text:
I went to a used car dealership recently, there's this guy in a tube suit waving around, and then there's these rows and rows of cars. And I always think that's a very philosophical place actually. Cause it really represents life and time. All of these cars were somebody's. They were either over-grown or neglected or loved. And I was just standing there in the sun, this huge expanse of asphalt. And all these cars with their stickers, their prices written in marker. And I thought, what an incredible compression of life in that sticker, in that price.
And I was looking for a car because my car has been acting up. The check engine light has been on, and it just barely starts. It acts very weird when it's braking or stopping or turning. It just feels a bit unreliable. And I don't want to buy a new car. I want to buy a used car. But I want something that is reliable.
So I walked around this place. And there was a guy named Daryl who came out to greet me. He's a salesman, very nice guy. And he walked me through the lot. And he gave me some history on a lot of these cars. This one is owned by a school teacher who only drives to church and that's it. This one is owned by a retiree who has every single receipt. This one was owned by a teenager, so he probably treats it like it's a game. And I liked one car in particular. It was a little silver car, and it smelled like lemon and coffee. And it started very nicely. It only has 89,000 miles. And I thought, wow, that's a lot of miles, but that's also nice, that it has a past. That it has been somewhere. That it has been used.
So we took it for a spin on the highway. And it was okay. It pulled a little bit to the right, but I pretended that I didn't notice it. And we drove around. And he talked to me about all the warranties, financing, whatever. And I asked him, did it have any accidents? And he said no. And I thought, I don't know whether I believe him or not. I think that's what makes used car buying fun and scary. You're just gonna trust somebody.
And then we negotiated in his office. And I had my car there as a trade-in. And I actually saw it from his office, and it looked so sad. But it was my car, and it carried me through so many things. My moves, my heartbreaks, my trips. It was like a little album, my car. But I traded it in, and we negotiated, and I bought the car.
And I drove off the lot. And I saw this tube man behind me, waving, selling air to no one. And I thought, we're all used cars in life, right? We come with miles, we come with bumps and bruises and scratches. We come with things we don't really disclose about our life. And we hope that somebody will look at us and still see value in us. And this car that I bought, it's not perfect. It rattles a little bit. It has a stain in the backseat that looks like a tiny country. But it starts in the morning. And that's what's important. It's not shiny, it's not new, it's not perfect. But it will start and take me somewhere. So that's enough. And I drove away with my windows open. I just felt so nice and happy.
And then I kept thinking about this. And I really feel that sometimes compromise is not a bad thing. That compromise can be a beautiful thing, that it's a way of getting things done when you can't have perfection. And I'm very happy that I bought this car. And the key in my pocket is a little scratched and battered, but it works. So I feel very happy.
